plan: Informative essay (CLD-P-ACT-E-000043) on Garrett Morgan's three-position traffic signal (1923 patent); topic checked against every ACT, SAT and ChatGPT verbal record (no Garrett Morgan or traffic-signal passage). Facts hedged ('reportedly' for the General Electric sale) and the essay states that Morgan did not invent the traffic signal. Ten items: supporting detail, dangling modifier, comma splice, concision, contrast transition, keep/delete, tense, precise wording, apostrophe, conclusion. Choice sets avoid contested comma rules (no choice depends on the comma before a compound predicate or a semicolon before a conjunction). Difficulty provisional. E043-04 and E043-08 withdrawn and dropped after both solvers flagged them (two defensible answers; redundant key text). Relabelled to the lower blind rating: E043-01 hard→easy, E043-02 hard→medium, E043-03 medium→easy, E043-06 hard→easy, E043-07 medium→easy, E043-10 medium→easy.

passages.title: The Third Position
passages.text:
[1] By the early 1920s, the streets of Cleveland, Ohio, were crowded with automobiles, horse-drawn wagons, bicycles, and pedestrians, all competing for the same space. [2] Some intersections had signals, but most of these could show only two commands: stop and go. [3] Because the signal switched instantly from one to the other, {{1|drivers already in the middle of an intersection had no warning that cross traffic was about to start}}.

[4] Garrett Morgan, a Cleveland inventor and businessman, had seen the danger firsthand. [5] {{2|Already known for a safety hood that firefighters and rescuers wore in smoke-filled spaces, his attention turned}} to the problem of the intersection. [6] His solution was a signal with a third position. [7] Before switching between stop and go, the signal would halt traffic in {{3|every direction, this gave}} drivers in the intersection time to clear it.

[8] Morgan received a patent for his design in 1923. [9] The signal itself was a T-shaped pole with arms that a person turned by hand, {{4|and so it}} looked little like the electric lights used today. [10] {{5|However,}} its central idea, a pause between stop and go, survives in the yellow light that appears at nearly every modern intersection.

[11] {{6|Morgan reportedly sold the rights to his signal to the General Electric Company for $40,000.}} [12] The sum allowed him to expand his other businesses, which included a newspaper and a company that made hair-care products. [13] Morgan {{7|has continued}} to work on inventions for the rest of his life, though none became as widely known as the signal.

[14] Historians are careful to note that Morgan did not invent the traffic signal; {{8|several earlier designs}} existed before his. [15] What he contributed was a solution to a specific problem that the earlier {{9|signals'}} had created. [16] {{10|In this way, his work shows how an invention can matter not because it is the first of its kind but because it fixes a flaw in what came before.}}

candidates.subskill: Choosing a detail that supports the paragraph's point
candidates.stem: Which choice most clearly explains why the two-position signals described in sentence 2 were dangerous?

choices.B: the signals were often mounted too high for pedestrians on the sidewalk to see clearly
choices.C: many drivers in Cleveland had only recently learned how to operate an automobile
choices.D: the signals had to be repainted every few years to keep their colors bright

candidates.evidence: Because the signal switched instantly from one to the other
candidates.explanation: The sentence begins by saying the signal switched instantly; the danger it creates is that drivers already in the intersection had no warning before cross traffic started.

B.rationale: This describes visibility for pedestrians, not the danger of switching instantly between stop and go.

C.rationale: This concerns drivers' experience, not the signal's instant switch.

D.rationale: Repainting has nothing to do with the danger of switching instantly.

hints: What problem does an instant switch create?

strategy.explanation: Check which choice follows from "switched instantly."

candidates.remember: A supporting detail must connect to the cause stated in the same sentence.

candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?

choices.B: Already known for a safety hood that firefighters and rescuers wore in smoke-filled spaces, the attention of Morgan turned
choices.C: Already known for a safety hood that firefighters and rescuers wore in smoke-filled spaces, Morgan turned his attention
choices.D: Already known for a safety hood that firefighters and rescuers wore in smoke-filled spaces, it was Morgan's attention that turned

candidates.evidence: to the problem of the intersection
candidates.explanation: The introductory phrase describes the person known for the safety hood, so "Morgan" must come right after the comma.

A.rationale: The opening phrase must describe Morgan, but the sentence makes it describe "his attention."

B.rationale: The opening phrase now describes "the attention," not Morgan.

D.rationale: The opening phrase now describes "it," not Morgan.

hints: Who was known for the safety hood?

strategy.explanation: Check what noun follows the opening phrase.

candidates.remember: An opening modifier describes the noun right after the comma.

candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
candidates.evidence: drivers in the intersection time to clear it
candidates.explanation: Both parts are independent clauses ("the signal would halt traffic in every direction" and "this gave drivers ... time to clear it"), so a semicolon correctly joins them.

A.rationale: "This gave drivers..." is an independent clause; joining it with only a comma creates a comma splice.

B.rationale: Without punctuation, the two independent clauses run together.

C.rationale: The comma wrongly separates the subject "This" from its verb "gave."

hints: Can the part after the comma stand alone?

strategy.explanation: Identify each clause's subject and verb.

candidates.remember: A comma alone cannot join two independent clauses.

candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
candidates.evidence: looked little like the electric lights used today
candidates.explanation: Sentence 9 says the device looked little like modern lights; sentence 10 says its idea survives anyway, so a contrast transition, "However," fits.

B.rationale: The sentence contrasts the old-fashioned device with its lasting idea; it is not similar to the previous sentence.

C.rationale: The sentence does not give an example of the previous sentence's point.

D.rationale: The survival of the yellow light is not caused by the signal's T-shaped pole.

hints: Do the two sentences agree or contrast?

strategy.explanation: Label the relationship before reading the choices.

candidates.remember: Use a contrast transition when a sentence turns against the one before it.

candidates.stem: The writer is considering deleting the underlined sentence. Should the sentence be kept or deleted?

choices.A: Deleted, because it shifts the focus from the signal to Morgan's other inventions.
choices.B: Deleted, because it repeats information given earlier in the essay about the patent.
choices.C: Kept, because it explains the source of the sum that the next sentence says helped Morgan's businesses.
choices.D: Kept, because it shows that Morgan's design was the first traffic signal ever built.

candidates.evidence: The sum allowed him to expand his other businesses
candidates.explanation: Sentence 12 refers to "The sum"; without sentence 11, the reader would not know what sum is meant.

A.rationale: The sentence is about selling the signal's rights, not about his other inventions.

B.rationale: The patent is mentioned earlier, but the sale and the sum are new information.

D.rationale: The essay says Morgan did not invent the traffic signal.

hints: What does "The sum" in sentence 12 refer to?

strategy.explanation: Check whether the next sentence depends on this one.

candidates.remember: Keep a sentence if a later sentence depends on it.

candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
candidates.evidence: to work on inventions for the rest of his life
candidates.explanation: The paragraph narrates past events in the simple past ("received," "sold," "allowed"), so "continued" keeps the tense consistent.

A.rationale: The present perfect "has continued" suggests the action is still going on, but the essay describes Morgan's past life.

C.rationale: The present tense does not fit an account of a life in the past.

D.rationale: The future tense does not fit an account of a life in the past.

hints: What tense does the paragraph use?

strategy.explanation: Match the tense of the surrounding sentences.

candidates.remember: Keep verb tenses consistent within a narrative.

candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
candidates.explanation: "Signals" is a plain plural noun here (the subject of "had created"), so it takes no apostrophe.

A.rationale: "Signals'" is possessive, but nothing follows that belongs to the signals.

B.rationale: "Signal's" is a singular possessive, but the word is the plural subject of "had created."

hints: Does anything belong to the signals?

strategy.explanation: Check whether a possessive is needed.

candidates.remember: Use an apostrophe only for possession or contraction.

candidates.subskill: Conclusion that states a larger point
candidates.stem: Which choice most effectively concludes the essay by stating a larger point that the essay's details support?

choices.B: Today, traffic engineers use computers to time signals at thousands of intersections in each large city.
choices.C: Cleveland, Ohio, is now home to many museums, parks, and universities that attract visitors every year.
choices.D: Morgan's newspaper continued to be published for many years after his death in 1963.

candidates.evidence: What he contributed was a solution to a specific problem
candidates.explanation: The essay argues that Morgan's contribution was fixing a flaw rather than being first; the current sentence states that larger point.

B.rationale: This describes modern traffic engineering, not a point that Morgan's story supports.

C.rationale: This shifts to the city and does not conclude the essay's discussion.

D.rationale: This adds a detail about the newspaper rather than a larger point about invention.

hints: What point does the last paragraph build toward?

strategy.explanation: Find the choice that generalizes from Morgan's story.

candidates.remember: A conclusion can state the larger lesson of the details.

withdrawn.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?

choices.C: and therefore, as a result, it
choices.D: and so, because of this, it

withdrawn.evidence: looked little like the electric lights used today
withdrawn.explanation: "So it" expresses the result clearly and concisely after the comma.

A.rationale: "And so" adds a conjunction that "so" already supplies.

C.rationale: "Therefore" and "as a result" repeat the same idea.

D.rationale: "Because of this" repeats the idea of "so."

hints: Do any words repeat an idea already expressed?

strategy.explanation: Choose the shortest choice that keeps the meaning.

withdrawn.remember: Cut words that repeat an idea.
withdrawn.withdrawn_reason: Both solvers: ", and so it" is acceptable standard English, so NO CHANGE and "so it" are both defensible. Dropped (not resubmitted).

withdrawn.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?

choices.D: several earlier designs that came before

withdrawn.explanation: "Several earlier designs existed before his" is precise and does not repeat itself.

C.rationale: "Things" is vague; the sentence is about earlier signal designs.

D.rationale: "Earlier" and "that came before" repeat the same idea, and "before his" follows.

hints: Does any choice say the same thing twice?
withdrawn.remember: Precise nouns beat vague ones like "things."
withdrawn.withdrawn_reason: Both solvers: the keyed text ("earlier designs existed before his") is itself slightly redundant. Dropped (not resubmitted).
